plain_english:
First, decide what kind of person you want to be. Then stick to that character whether you're alone or with others.

Stay quiet most of the time. When you do speak, keep it necessary and brief. Sure, you can join conversations when the moment calls for it. But don't get caught up in the usual topics — sports, food, drink, and all that everyday chatter. And especially don't talk about other people, whether you're criticizing them, praising them, or comparing them. If you can steer the conversation toward better topics, do it. If you're stuck with strangers, just stay quiet.

Don't laugh too loud, too often, or too much.

Avoid making promises or swearing oaths if you can help it. At least try to keep them to a minimum.
original_excerpt: Begin by prescribing to yourself some character and demeanor, such as you may preserve both alone and in company.

plain_english:
Stay away from cheap, lowbrow entertainment. But if you have to go, pay attention so you don't slip into that mindset without realizing it. Even if you're a decent person, spending time with corrupt people will corrupt you too.

Give your body only what it absolutely needs — food, drink, clothes, shelter, basic help. Cut out anything that's just for show or luxury.

Before marriage, avoid sleeping with women. But don't be harsh or judgmental toward those who do. And don't keep bragging that you don't.
original_excerpt: Be mostly silent, or speak merely what is needful, and in few words. We may, however, enter sparingly into discourse sometimes, when occasion calls for it; but let it not run on any of the common subjects, as gladiators, or horse races, or athletic champions, or food, or drink—the vulgar topics of conversation—and especially not on men, so as either to blame, or praise, or make comparisons. If you are able, then, by your own conversation, bring over that of your company to proper subjects; but if you happen to find yourself among strangers, be silent.

plain_english: If someone tells you that someone else is talking badly about you, don't defend yourself against what was said. Instead, say: "He doesn't know about my other flaws, or he wouldn't have stuck to just those ones."
original_excerpt: Let not your laughter be loud, frequent, or abundant.

plain_english:
You don't need to go to public events very often. But when you do go, don't care more about anyone else than yourself. Want things to happen exactly as they do. Want the best person to win. This way, nothing will disappoint you. Don't cheer loudly, don't mock anyone, and don't get carried away with strong emotions. When you leave, don't talk endlessly about what happened if it doesn't help you improve as a person. All that chatter just shows the spectacle impressed you too much.

Don't be eager to attend private readings and performances. If you do go, stay serious and dignified. But don't make yourself unpleasant to be around.
original_excerpt: Avoid taking oaths, if possible, altogether; at any rate, so far as you are able.

plain_english:
When you're about to meet with someone, especially someone who seems more important than you, ask yourself how Socrates or Zeno would handle it. This way you won't be lost when things don't go as planned.

When you're going to see someone powerful, imagine ahead of time that they might not be there. They might not let you in. The doors might stay closed. They might ignore you completely. If you still need to go despite all this, accept whatever happens. Don't tell yourself afterward, "That wasn't worth it." That kind of thinking is cheap and shows you're letting outside things control you.
original_excerpt: Avoid public and vulgar entertainments; but if ever an occasion calls you to them, keep your attention upon the stretch, that you may not imperceptibly slide into vulgarity. For be assured that if a person be ever so pure himself, yet, if his companion be corrupted, he who converses with him will be corrupted likewise.

plain_english: When you're with other people, don't constantly talk about your own achievements and adventures. Sure, you might enjoy reliving your exciting moments, but others don't want to hear your stories all the time. Also, don't try too hard to make people laugh. You might end up being crude or vulgar. Plus, it can make people respect you less. Be careful around inappropriate conversations too. When someone starts talking inappropriately, speak up and tell them to stop. Or at least stay quiet, look uncomfortable, and let them know you don't approve.
original_excerpt: Provide things relating to the body no further than absolute need requires, as meat, drink, clothing, house, retinue. But cut off everything that looks toward show and luxury.

plain_english: Before you get married, do everything you can to avoid sleeping with women you shouldn't. But don't be harsh or judgmental toward people who do this. And don't keep bragging that you're better than them.
original_excerpt: Before marriage guard yourself with all your ability from unlawful intercourse with women; yet be not uncharitable or severe to those who are led into this, nor boast frequently that you yourself do otherwise.

plain_english: If someone tells you that a person is talking badly about you, don't defend yourself against what they said. Instead, say: "He doesn't know about my other faults, or he wouldn't have only mentioned those ones."
original_excerpt: If anyone tells you that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses about what is said of you, but answer: "He was ignorant of my other faults, else he would not have mentioned these alone."

plain_english: You don't need to go to public events very often. But if there's a good reason to attend, don't care more about anyone else than yourself. Just want things to happen as they do, and hope the best person wins. This way, nothing will disappoint you. But don't cheer, boo, or get worked up at all. And when you leave, don't talk endlessly about what happened if it doesn't help you improve. Talking like that just shows you were impressed by the spectacle.
original_excerpt: It is not necessary for you to appear often at public spectacles; but if ever there is a proper occasion for you to be there, do not appear more solicitous for any other than for yourself—that is, wish things to be only just as they are, and only the best man to win; for thus nothing will go against you. But abstain entirely from acclamations and derision and violent emotions. And when you come away, do not discourse a great deal on what has passed and what contributes nothing to your own amendment. For it would appear by such discourse that you were dazzled by the show.

plain_english: Don't be eager to attend private readings and performances. But if you do go, keep your composure and dignity. Just don't be unpleasant about it.
original_excerpt: Be not prompt or ready to attend private recitations; but if you do attend, preserve your gravity and dignity, and yet avoid making yourself disagreeable.

plain_english: When you're about to meet with someone, especially someone who seems more important than you, ask yourself how Socrates or Zeno would handle it. You won't be confused about how to act when things come up.
original_excerpt: When you are going to confer with anyone, and especially with one who seems your superior, represent to yourself how Socrates or Zeno would behave in such a case, and you will not be at a loss to meet properly whatever may occur.

plain_english: When you're about to meet someone powerful, imagine the worst first. Maybe they won't be there. Maybe you'll be turned away at the door. Maybe they'll ignore you completely. If you still need to go despite all this, then accept whatever happens. Don't tell yourself afterward, "That wasn't worth the trouble." That's petty thinking. It's what people do when they let outside things control them.
original_excerpt: When you are going before anyone in power, fancy to yourself that you may not find him at home, that you may be shut out, that the doors may not be opened to you, that he may not notice you. If, with all this, it be your duty to go, bear what happens and never say to yourself, "It was not worth so much"; for this is vulgar, and like a man bewildered by externals.

plain_english: When you're with other people, don't constantly talk about your own accomplishments and close calls. You might enjoy reliving your adventures, but others don't enjoy hearing them nearly as much. Also avoid trying too hard to make people laugh. You might slip into crude humor, and you could end up looking foolish to your friends. Stay away from dirty jokes and inappropriate topics too. When someone starts heading in that direction, speak up and correct them if you get the chance. Or at least stay quiet, look embarrassed, and make it clear with your expression that you don't approve of that kind of talk.
original_excerpt: In company, avoid a frequent and excessive mention of your own actions and dangers. For however agreeable it may be to yourself to allude to the risks you have run, it is not equally agreeable to others to hear your adventures. Avoid likewise an endeavor to excite laughter, for this may readily slide you into vulgarity, and, besides, may be apt to lower you in the esteem of your acquaintance. Approaches to indecent discourse are likewise dangerous. Therefore, when anything of this sort happens, use the first fit opportunity to rebuke him who makes advances that way, or, at least, by silence and blushing and a serious look show yourself to be displeased by such talk.
